text: This distinction is highly relevant to yoga practice, where the exact same external posture can be achieved through markedly different internal control strategies. One mode may involve forceful muscular contraction without deliberate effort modulation, resulting in rigid stabilization and heightened corrective control. Another mode may deliberately minimize unnecessary effort through refined postural organization. Although these two modes appear externally identical biomechanically, they may reflect fundamentally different physiological states and central regulatory architectures. Importantly, this efficiency does not represent passive relaxation or fully automatic subcortical habit. Instead, it reflects a refined regulatory organization involving economical, real-time cortical modulation capable of minimizing control burden while preserving active task engagement. A systematic review which compared different styles of yoga (ashtanga, Bikram, gentle, hatha, Iyengar, power and vinyasa) indicates that metabolic and heart rate responses vary across yoga styles and asana ( Forseth and Hunter, 2020 ).
source_label: Relaxation in action: enhanced vagal modulation during Virabhadrasana (a standing yoga-asana) despite orthostatic demand suggests efficient regulation of effort
